mcqs.question: Why does synchronous replication add latency to every write?
options: Because the leader waits for one or more followers to confirm the write before reporting success to the client
Because synchronous replication requires encrypting data twice
Because it only works with a single follower and no leader at all
Because it always writes to disk before writing to memory
mcqs.explanation: The added latency comes directly from waiting on follower confirmation before acknowledging the client — that round trip is the cost. It doesn't involve double encryption, it works with a leader and any number of followers, and disk-vs-memory ordering isn't the mechanism.

mcqs.question: What can happen under asynchronous replication if the leader crashes immediately after acknowledging a write?
options: Nothing — asynchronous replication guarantees the write already reached a follower
The write can be permanently lost, even though the client was told it succeeded
The write is automatically retried by the client's driver until it succeeds
All followers immediately become unreadable until the leader recovers
mcqs.explanation: Asynchronous replication acknowledges as soon as the leader alone has the write, before any follower confirms — so a leader crash right after can lose that write entirely. There's no automatic client retry from this alone, and followers remain readable, just potentially stale.

mcqs.question: A user posts a comment, then immediately reloads and doesn't see it, though it appears seconds later. What's the most likely cause?
options: The write was permanently lost and then somehow recovered
The reload request hit a follower that was still behind the leader due to replication lag
The database schema doesn't support comments
The user's browser cached an old version of the entire page
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook replication-lag symptom: the read landed on a follower that hadn't caught up yet, and it resolved once the follower replicated the write. It wasn't data loss, a schema issue, or purely a browser cache problem.

mcqs.question: Your service load-balances reads across several asynchronous replicas. A user's own recent write sometimes appears missing right after they make it. What's the most direct fix?
options: Switch every replica to synchronous replication
Tell users to wait 30 seconds before reloading any page
Route that user's post-write reads to the leader or a replica known to be caught up, instead of any load-balanced replica
Remove read replicas entirely and serve all reads from the leader permanently
mcqs.explanation: The targeted fix is routing the specific read-your-writes case to a known-current source, not converting the whole system to synchronous (an unnecessary latency cost everywhere) or removing replicas altogether (losing the scaling benefit they exist for).
